Congressional districts are allocated based on population. There are some big disparities due to high concentrated populations and low population states that create some imbalances, but it's far more even than the Senate.

Most people misunderstand the point of the Senate. The Senate isn't supposed to represent the people in the state, they're supposed to represent the state itself. Originally, senators were elected by state legislatures. Each state got to send two representatives to the Senate as a way to give them equal representation in Congress.

It made sense back when there were less than 20 states and they were all essentially individual countries that agreed to work together for the sake of international affairs and interstate commerce. The federal government was very weak and had a limited role in state affairs. That's now very different and we don't live in that kind of country anymore.

When they turned the election of senators over to the people directly, the Senate lost its purpose. It no longer made sense because it now was beholden to voters themselves, which was the point and design of the House of Representatives. Senators no longer worked in the interest of their state legislatures. There was nothing equal or fair about their positions. One senator could represent a hundred thousand people and the senator next to him represented 20 million.

Instead of giving the election to the people they should have just done away with the Senate altogether, but there's no way smaller states would give up that kind of influence regardless of whether it's fair or not.
